o: If every component has value v, then v divides the total sum S and the number of components is S/v, so we may delete at most S/v − 1 edges. Since nums[i] ≤ 50 and n ≤ 2·10⁴, S ≤ 10⁶, giving few candidate divisors. For each divisor v of S, greedily DFS: accumulate subtree sums; whenever a subtree sums to exactly v, cut it off (increment cut count, return 0 upward). The value v is achievable iff the number of cuts equals S/v. Example 1: S=14, v=6 isn't a divisor... actually components of value 6 with three components need S=18? Here S=6+2+2+2+6=18, v=6, cuts=2 ✓.
k: Component value must divide S; candidates are divisors of S with S/v ≤ n.
Greedy cutting works: if any subtree sum exceeds v without hitting it, that v is infeasible — the cut count check catches this.
Only divisors need testing: O(√S · n) ≈ fast enough.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate divisors + greedy subtree cutting
a.i: For each divisor v of S, run a DFS returning each subtree's residual sum; cut (reset to 0) whenever the sum reaches v. Feasible iff final cut count equals S/v.
s: Compute S = sum(nums); iterate v over divisors of S (both v and S/v up to √S).
DFS from node 0: sum = nums[u] + Σ children residuals; if sum == v, count a cut and return 0; else return sum.
v is valid iff cuts == S/v; answer = max over valid v of S/v − 1.
a.t: O(√S · n) — each divisor candidate triggers one O(n) DFS; S ≤ 10⁶ so about 10⁴–10⁵ operations per divisor family, well within limits.
a.sp: O(n) for adjacency and recursion stack.

w: This single approach is the standard optimal one. Pitfalls: forgetting to test both v and S/v when enumerating divisors, deep recursion in Python (raise the recursion limit or convert to iterative DFS), and the n=1 edge case (answer 0). Follow-up: handle negative values, or a graph with cycles (becomes NP-hard in general — worth mentioning).
